value.overview: The Spotted Woodcreeper is a medium-sized, forest-dwelling songbird in the ovenbird family. It climbs tree trunks and large limbs while searching for insects and other small prey in bark, moss, and epiphytes. Its olive-brown plumage, pale spotting, buffy eye-ring, and spotted underparts provide useful identification marks. The species occurs from Mexico through Central America to western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador, with Costa Rica forming an important part of its resident range.
value.classification: The Spotted Woodcreeper belongs to the family Furnariidae and subfamily Dendrocolaptinae, the woodcreepers. Some taxonomic systems separate northern and southern populations; Xiphorhynchus erythropygius is generally treated as the northern Spotted Woodcreeper in global assessments.
value.identification: This woodcreeper is about 22–24 cm long, with a fairly heavy, straight bill and a long, stiff tail used for support while climbing. Adults are mainly olive-brown, with pale buff or yellowish spotting on the breast and belly, subdued streaking on the back, and a noticeable buffy eye-ring. The throat and head are also marked with diffuse pale spots or streaks. Juveniles are generally browner and have less distinct underpart markings.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, with related populations continuing into western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a permanent resident, relatively common at middle elevations on the Caribbean slope and in southern Pacific regions, but largely absent from the dry northwestern forests. It is most frequent around 700–1,450 m and may occur locally to about 1,700 m. It uses humid evergreen and montane forest, forest edges, older secondary growth, and some tree plantations.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it is not considered a long-distance migrant. Individuals may move locally with food availability or mixed-species flocks.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but in Costa Rica nesting has been reported mainly from March through June. The nest is placed in a cavity, hollow, stump, or crevice, often in a palm stump or other tree structure, at roughly 2–9 m above the ground. A clutch commonly contains two eggs. Details of incubation, nestling care, and fledging are poorly documented, and both adults are believed to participate in raising the young.
value.dietFeeding: The Spotted Woodcreeper mainly searches for arthropods and other small invertebrates on trunks, branches, bark, moss, and epiphyte-covered surfaces. It climbs upward along tree trunks and limbs, probing crevices with its bill and occasionally reaching into foliage. It usually forages in the upper understory and canopy. Individuals may also follow army-ant swarms, taking prey disturbed by the ants, and sometimes feed as members of mixed-species forest flocks.
value.behavior: It is usually seen alone or in pairs, moving methodically up trunks and branches with its stiff tail pressed against the surface. The species can join mixed-species flocks and may travel between the upper understory and canopy while foraging. It is generally vocal, especially around dawn and dusk, when it gives repeated descending whistles. Although it uses forest edges and older secondary growth, it remains associated with habitats retaining substantial tree cover and epiphytes.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been reliably quantified. Available assessments describe the population as believed to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and is locally common in suitable habitat.
